verdict: OK to lend in Bengaluru machine tools — back established component and sub-assembly makers selling into the local OEM build-out, structure against inventory and receivable cycles, and decline thin-capitalised traders and stressed PSU-linked names.
title: Bengaluru machine tools: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A machine-tool unit converts castings, spindles, drives and controllers into a machine that a customer uses to cut metal, and cash comes back only after the machine is built, dispatched, installed and accepted.** Build cycles are long and lumpy — peer management flags that large machines take longer to build and revenue recognition slips [4]. So when a proposal lands, check the order book's age and the acceptance/installation terms, not just the invoice pipeline.

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in the controller and precision sub-assemblies; cash sits in work-in-progress and receivables, not in the shop floor.** Peers show the operating leverage is real when volumes run — Macpower posted Q2 FY27 revenue of Rs 120.33 crore, up 40.39% YoY, at a 16.56% EBITDA margin [5], while Jyoti's Q1 FY27 standalone revenue grew 37% to Rs 107 crore [7]. But a rating report on a peer flags continuing overdrawals of more than 30 days in cash credit and an elongated receivables cycle [9] — so when a proposal lands, check CC utilisation and debtor days first; if the CC account has been overdrawn beyond 30 days, ask for the receivable ageing and the top-five buyer payment record before anything else.

## What has changed now
**Bengaluru has just become a machine-tool production city, not only a buyer city.** DN Solutions opened its first India plant here at an investment of Rs 600 crore [2], with local production of machining and turning centres [1]. Separately, Ethereal Machines raised $28.5 million Series B to build a mega factory near Bengaluru and develop a multi-axis CNC controller [3]. The demand backdrop is firm: IIP for NIC 28 output is +10.3% YoY and +10.4% Apr-to-date [D], and Karnataka's GST collections are running +11.1% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D]. Note the rating reports [8][9][10][11] carry no clear date and should be read as background, not current.

## Who to pursue, who to avoid
**Pursue tier-2 component and sub-assembly makers — castings, sheet-metal enclosures, spindles, tooling — that sell to the incoming OEM and to established machine builders, plus machining-as-a-service shops with a controller of their own.** Avoid pure traders of imported machines and thin-capitalised assemblers with no controller capability; the import-substitution room peers describe [4] accrues to firms with design depth, not to resellers.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the cycle: cash credit sized to a documented WIP-plus-receivable cycle, a term loan matched to the machine's build-and-acceptance timeline, and a monthly stock-and-debtor statement as a condition.** Take the order book position, CC utilisation and debtor ageing every month. If inventory has been built ahead of a ramp-up — as one peer has done for its 10,000-machine expansion [4] — ask what funds the carrying cost.
watch: overdrawn beyond 30 days or debtor days rising -> freeze enhancement, seek receivable-backed structure
acceptance slippage or cancellations -> re-rate the borrower's cycle and resize limits
stock rising faster than dispatches -> ask what funds the carrying cost
single buyer above half of sales -> cap exposure and seek diversification plan
